result: The authors identified the first short linear sequences (DegV1, a 4X repeat of IHPYW) that function as degrons from the ER lumen, facilitating proteasomal degradation through ERAD when transferred to proteins. These degrons enable degradation of both luminal and integral membrane ER proteins.
evaluation: The editor states this is an 'important study' that 'identifies a short amino acid sequence' functioning as a 'degron for ER proteins' and provides 'solid evidence.' Reviewers confirm the authors 'convincingly show' the degron targets ER proteins for degradation with 'well-founded' data and 'appropriate controls.' All reviewers accept the core finding without challenging its validity.

result: Using a pentapeptide library screen with FACS sorting, the authors identified sequences enriched in unstable proteins, particularly those beginning with isoleucine (3.8-fold enrichment) and leucine (1.6-fold enrichment). Multimerization of the IHPYW sequence (4X repeat) dramatically decreased protein stability.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the screening approach and findings without criticism. One reviewer notes the authors 'use a previously established reporter' and 'determine the stability of these constructs in a high throughput FACS-sorting procedure' to 'identify a set of peptides.' The methodology and results are accepted as technically sound.

result: DegV1 functions as an ER luminal degron only when positioned at the N-terminus of ER-localized proteins. Internal or C-terminal placement of DegV1 did not affect protein stability.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding without challenge. One reviewer explicitly states 'the degrons only functioned when placed at the N-terminus of the target protein.' The position-dependent activity is accepted as demonstrated by the data.

result: DegV1-targeted luminal ER substrates are degraded by the proteasome through the Hrd1-ERAD pathway. Components of the ERAD-L complex (Hrd1, Hrd3, Der1, Usa1) except Yos9 were required for DegV1 degradation, while Doa10 was not required.
evaluation: Reviewers confirm the authors 'demonstrated that degradation was via the ERAD pathway' and note the degron 'utilizes components of the Hrd1 ubiquitin ligase complex.' The editor states the sequence 'initiates proteasomal degradation via the Hrd1 ER quality control ubiquitin ligase complex.' The mechanistic characterization is accepted.

result: DegV1 functions as an N-terminal degron for endogenous proteins with diverse topologies, including the luminal protein Suc2, single-pass membrane protein Big1, and multi-spanning membrane protein Elo1. Degradation is proteasome-dependent as shown by bortezomib sensitivity.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the authors 'identified a sequence that can be appended onto other ER targeted proteins to mediate their degradation' and that it 'targets other ER proteins with different topological and folding properties.' The data showing degradation of diverse protein types is accepted as supportive of the conclusions.

result: DegV1 functions as an Hrd1-dependent ER-localized degron in mammalian cells (U2OS), with ER-DegV1-mNG showing instability (half-life ~4 hr) that is reversed by proteasome inhibition (bortezomib) or p97 inhibition (CB5083), and stabilized in Hrd1 knockout cells.
evaluation: Reviewers note 'the degron also targets ER-proteins in mammalian cells' without expressing doubt. The editor acknowledges the work demonstrates conservation across eukaryotes. The mammalian cell data is accepted as extending the yeast findings.

result: The IHPYW sequence forming DegV1 is uncommon in nature, absent from S. cerevisiae and fungal genomes, yet degron-containing proteins show degradation rates similar to well-characterized ERAD substrates, suggesting DegV1 is degraded in a manner consistent with endogenous ERAD substrates.
evaluation: One reviewer raises concern that 'the DegV1 sequence used throughout the paper is not present in any yeast or fungal proteins' and questions whether 'such sequences function in vivo,' stating 'the role of such sequences in vivo is questionable.' The editor notes 'the in vivo relevance of the findings' requires future work. This creates uncertainty about physiological relevance despite technical validity.

result: The authors speculate about whether DegV1-tagged proteins are transported in a folded or unfolded state, favoring the idea that proteins are recognized and transported in an unfolded state after ERAD complex engagement.
evaluation: One reviewer notes 'the fact that it has to be located at the N-terminus of the protein to induce degradation is at odds with the idea that proteins to be degraded need to be unfolded,' highlighting a conceptual tension. The editor states 'future work is required to obtain a more detailed view of the properties of this degron' and 'the mechanisms underlying its recognition.' These mechanistic questions remain unresolved.

result: Background claims about degrons, the ubiquitin proteasome system, ERAD pathways, and the Hrd1 complex composition establish the context that all previously identified degrons function in the cytosol.
evaluation: These are background/contextual claims supported by citations. Reviewers do not challenge these established facts and use them as the basis for understanding the novelty of the work. The editor and reviewers accept the premise that prior degrons were cytosolic.

result: Approximately 90% of the ER-targeted construct had the signal sequence removed, indicating uncleaved signal sequence was unlikely to factor into DegV1 function.
evaluation: This technical detail about signal sequence cleavage is presented with supporting data (Figure 2A) and is not questioned by reviewers. It serves as a control to ensure the degron effect is not due to uncleaved signal sequences.
